sp25_mt2_E2.1.title: E2.1 - Sum of Two Periodic Signals
sp25_mt2_E2.1.description: Analyzes the periodicity of the sum of two periodic discrete-time signals with different fundamental periods. Explores how the periods combine under addition.
concepts: Periodicity definition: x[n+p] = x[n] for all n ∈ ℤ

problem_statement.setup: Two periodic signals x[n] with period p and y[n] with period q. Define z[n] = x[n] + y[n].
problem_statement.part_a: If p and q are coprime, find period r of z[n]
problem_statement.part_b: If p = 2k and q = 2ℓ where k,ℓ are coprime, find smallest r
problem_statement.part_c: For x[n] = cos(3π/4 · n) and y[n] = sin(3π/5 · n), find period of z[n]

part_a.explanation: When p and q are coprime, lcm(p,q) = pq. Since x[n+pq] = x[n] and y[n+pq] = y[n], we have z[n+pq] = x[n+pq] + y[n+pq] = x[n] + y[n] = z[n].
part_a.key_insight: For coprime integers, LCM equals their product

part_b.explanation: With p = 2k and q = 2ℓ where gcd(k,ℓ) = 1, we have lcm(p,q) = lcm(2k, 2ℓ) = 2·lcm(k,ℓ) = 2kℓ
part_b.key_insight: Factor out common factors before computing LCM

steps: For x[n] = cos(3π/4 · n): Given p = 8
For y[n] = sin(3π/5 · n): Find q using ω₀ = 2π/N
sin(3π/5 · n) has period when 3π/5 · q = 2πm for integer m

sp25_mt2_E2.2.title: E2.2 - Signal Fusion in Self-Driving Cars
sp25_mt2_E2.2.description: Applies Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization to sensor signals from LiDAR, Radar, and GPS to remove correlation and improve signal discrimination.

problem_statement.part_a: Compute cos(θᵢⱼ) for all pairs, identify largest/smallest overlaps
problem_statement.part_b: Apply Gram-Schmidt to obtain orthonormal vectors q₁, q₂, q₃

part_a.answer: Largest positive overlap: a₁,a₃ (cos θ = 1/2). Largest negative: a₂,a₃ (cos θ = -1/2). Least overlap: a₁,a₂ (cos θ = 0, already orthogonal)

step3.description: Orthogonalize a₃ against q₁ and q₂

part_b.verification: All qᵢ have ||qᵢ|| = 1 and ⟨qᵢ,qⱼ⟩ = 0 for i≠j

sp25_mt2_E2.3.title: E2.3 - Robot Motion in 2D
sp25_mt2_E2.3.description: Studies 2D transformations using homogeneous coordinates: rotation and translation. Examines non-commutativity of transformation compositions.

problem_statement.part_a: Find position after rotation then translation
problem_statement.part_b: Find position after translation then rotation

part_c.explanation: Matrix multiplication is not commutative: TR ≠ RT in general. Geometrically, rotating then translating produces a different result than translating then rotating because rotation happens about the origin.
part_c.example: From parts (a) and (b): (2,4) ≠ (-3,5), confirming order matters

formulas: Rotation by θ: R(θ) = [[cos θ, -sin θ, 0],[sin θ, cos θ, 0],[0,0,1]]
sp25_mt2_E2.3.note: This problem uses homogeneous coordinates, which is a fundamental topic in computer graphics, but since it's primarily about matrix transformations and NOT about signal processing topics, it could be classified as 'vectors-matrices' or excluded depending on curriculum focus.

sp25_mt2_E2.4.title: E2.4 - Orthonormal Basis Decomposition
sp25_mt2_E2.4.description: Verifies orthonormality of a basis and decomposes a vector into this basis. Connects to Parseval's theorem for energy conservation.

problem_statement.part_a: Prove {φ₁,φ₂,φ₃} forms orthonormal basis for ℝ³
problem_statement.part_b: Find X₁,X₂,X₃ for x = [3,4,12]ᵀ = X₁φ₁ + X₂φ₂ + X₃φ₃

part_a.conclusion: All vectors have unit length and are mutually orthogonal, forming an orthonormal basis.

part_b.verification: x = X₁φ₁ + X₂φ₂ + X₃φ₃ should equal [3,4,12]ᵀ

formulas: Decomposition coefficients: Xᵢ = ⟨x,φᵢ⟩ when basis is orthonormal
Parseval's identity: ||x||² = Σᵢ|Xᵢ|² for orthonormal basis

sp25_mt2_E2.5.title: E2.5 - Discrete-Time Fourier Series (DTFS)
sp25_mt2_E2.5.description: Computes DTFS coefficients for a periodic signal and expresses it in closed form using complex exponentials and Euler's formula.
concepts: DTFS synthesis equation: x[n] = Σₖ Xₖe^(jkω₀n)
Euler's formula: e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ

problem_statement.signal: Periodic signal with period p=4, values: x[0]=2, x[1]=-1, x[2]=-1, x[3]=2 (repeating)
problem_statement.part_a: Find all DTFS coefficients Xₖ for k ∈ ⟨4⟩
problem_statement.part_b: Express x[n] = α + β cos(πn) and find α, β

coefficient_X3.note: By conjugate symmetry for real signals: X₃ = X₁*

part_b.alternative: If required form is x[n] = α + β cos(πn)
part_b.check_period_2: cos(πn) has period 2, but signal has period 4
part_b.answer: α = 1/2, β depends on how we interpret. The signal contains frequency components at ω=0 and ω=π/2, not just ω=π.

formulas: Euler: e^(jθ) = cos θ + j sin θ

sp25_mt2_E2.6.title: E2.6 - Matching Null Spaces
sp25_mt2_E2.6.description: Proves the fundamental result that N(A) = N(AᵀA), establishing equivalence of null spaces. Important for understanding least squares and fundamental subspaces.
concepts: Set equality: S = T iff S ⊆ T and T ⊆ S

problem_statement.theorem: For matrix A ∈ ℝᵐˣⁿ, prove N(A) = N(AᵀA)

part_a.goal: If x ∈ N(A), then x ∈ N(AᵀA)
proof: Multiply both sides by Aᵀ: Aᵀ(Ax) = Aᵀ(0)
part_a.key_step: Left-multiplying by Aᵀ preserves the zero

part_b.goal: If x ∈ N(AᵀA), then x ∈ N(A)

conclusion.result: Since N(A) ⊆ N(AᵀA) and N(AᵀA) ⊆ N(A), we have N(A) = N(AᵀA)
conclusion.significance: This is crucial for least squares: minimizing ||Ax-b|| leads to solving AᵀAx = Aᵀb. Solutions exist when b - Ax ⊥ N(A) = N(AᵀA).
